23.3 c hi-s quare a nalysis of Missing d ata
In many data collection situations, particularly those involving human beings as the exper-
imental units, missing values carry as much information as complete responses. If many
274 n n n r e S earch Metho DS for Infor M at I on Sy S te MS n ch apter 23
people refuse to answer questions on a particular topic, this suggests that the topic is sensi-
tive and perhaps important, and it may deserve further study.
Chi-square tests of independence can be used to analyze the missing values in a file in an
exploratory way, by detecting significant dependence between the missing values of one
variable and responses or nonresponses to another. If such a dependence is found, further
qualitative (nonstatistical) analysis might explain the connection.
Datafiles can be broken down by variables, by cases, and by subfiles (subsets of the file).
Exploratory chi-square analysis of missing data includes tests of independence for variable
versus variable and for subfile versus variable. The contingency tables for such tests will have
the form shown in Table 23.5.

Regression and Curve Fitting
A CER is a mathematical expression, expressing cost as a function of one or more cost driv-
ing variables. In fact, the problem is that the CER complexity increases as one moves from
linear to non-linear relationship, and from a single cost driver to more than one cost driver.
But today, the necessary algorithms are well-known and widely available. The main meth-
ods to curve fitting are the multivariate regression techniques and cost improvement curve
analysis. With the use of modern computer tools, it is possible to automatically investigate
and test many combinations of CER’s mathematical forms (linear, logarithm, exponential).
One can also use more advanced black-box modeling techniques such as neural networks if
the loss of the readability of the cost model is acceptable.
Test of the CERs Statistical Quality
Finally, we must verify the significance and accuracy of the cost estimation models through
various statistical tests. The choice of the cost drivers can be statistically established and
tested here. The CER can be simplified by selecting only the most statistically significant
terms, for example by using stepwise regression techniques.
Selection of the Best CER
At this point, it is usual to obtain a great number of candidate models. In many cases, the
statistical regression quality and estimation criteria are not sufficient. For their validation,
the CERs must demonstrate reliability for an acceptable number of trials, and they should
be representative of the database domain of application. It is also necessary to consider the
technical coherence of the CER as defined by the experts in the application domain. At
last, some input variables in the multiple regression do not have an important explanatory
effect on the response. Then, it is a convenient simplification to keep only the statistically
significant cost drivers in the model. The stepwise regression starts with all the terms in the
model and removes the least significant terms until all the remaining terms are statistically
significant. It is also possible to start with a subset of all the terms and then add significant
terms or remove insignificant.
This illustration shows how linear statistical models for regression, analysis of variance, and
experimental designs are widely used today in management. The next three units present a
unified approach to the application of linear statistical models in regression, then in analysis
of variance, and finally in experimental designs. The notion of a general linear statistical
model which arises naturally in the context of regression models, is carried over to analysis of
variance and experimental design. Application of the approach is readily understandable and

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 24.1 Introduction
chunks.content:
24.1 Introduction
In Unit 5, we saw that the chi-square test of independence can be used to detect a relation-
ship between two variables. When such a test reveals a dependence, however, it tells us noth-
ing about the nature of the relationship. Is it strong or weak? Do large values of one variable
generally correspond to large or small values of the other? In this chapter, we will develop
numerical measures of the correlation between the values of two variables.

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: 24.2 Scatter Diagrams
chunks.content:
24.2 Scatter Diagrams
We have seen how useful histograms can be in visualizing the distribution of the values of
a variable. Similarly, we can create a graphical display of the values of two variables that
illustrates the nature and degree of any relationship they may share. Such displays are called
scatter diagrams, and are formed by plotting in the XY plane points whose coordinates are
the paired values of the two variables. When one variable is thought to be dependent on the
other, the values of the dependent variable are plotted along the vertical (Y) axis, while the
values of the independent variable are plotted on the horizontal (X) axis.
For example, Table 24.1 gives values of floor area and natural gas used in January for
15 Midwestern homes heated with natural gas.
